real_title: Avon Freeholds Limited v Cresta Court E RTM Company Limited
anonymised_title: The Freeholder v The RTM Company
facts: The Freeholder owns the freehold of a building containing 20 flats. The RTM Company is a right to manage company incorporated by leaseholders to acquire the right to manage the building under Chapter 1 of Part 2 of the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Act 2002 (the 2002 Act). On 4 November 2021 the RTM Company gave notices of invitation to participate (NIPs) to all those it had identified as qualifying tenants who were not yet members. It did not give a NIP to one qualifying tenant, who held a 150-year lease granted in 2020 whose registration was still pending. It is now common ground that she was a qualifying tenant throughout. On 21 January 2022 the RTM Company served its claim notice on the Freeholder. That date was the relevant date. On 26 January 2022 the tenant agreed to become a member of the RTM Company and signified her support for the claim. She has never complained about the lack of a NIP and was not a party to the litigation. It is agreed that on the relevant date all the substantive eligibility conditions in sections 72 to 77 and section 79(3) to (5) were met, including the requirement that at least half of the qualifying tenants were members. It is also agreed that the RTM Company had not complied with section 78(1), which requires a NIP to be given to each eligible qualifying tenant before a claim is made. Nor had it complied with section 79(2), which provides that the claim notice may not be given unless each person required to be given a NIP has been given one at least 14 days before. On 24 February 2022 the Freeholder served a counter-notice. The only ground still live is the failure to give the tenant a NIP. The RTM Company applied to the First-tier Tribunal (FtT) for a determination that it was entitled to acquire the right to manage. The FtT found for the RTM Company, and the Upper Tribunal upheld that decision. The Court of Appeal allowed the Freeholder's appeal. It held that the claim notice was invalid and a nullity because it had been given in breach of section 79(2), so the claim could not succeed. The RTM Company appeals to the Supreme Court.

issues.question: Does a failure by an RTM company to give a notice of invitation to participate to a qualifying tenant, in breach of sections 78(1) and 79(2) of the 2002 Act, invalidate the claim notice or otherwise prevent the RTM company from being entitled to acquire the right to manage, so that a landlord can rely on it in a counter-notice under section 84(2)(b)?

Is the statement in A1 Properties (Sunderland) Ltd v Tudor Studios RTM Co Ltd [2024] UKSC 27 at para 69, that section 79(2) means no valid claim notice can be given if NIPs have not been given, part of the ratio decidendi of that case, or otherwise a statement this Court should follow here?

appellant_submissions: The RTM Company argues that the right to manage scheme is divided into entitlement conditions of substance and a procedural code. A counter-notice under section 84(2)(b) must allege that the company was not entitled to acquire the right to manage, and that concerns substance rather than procedure. Sections 78(1) and 79(2) are procedural. They protect qualifying tenants, who have no right to object to a claim or to give a counter-notice. The Freeholder is not within the class the rules protect and suffered no prejudice. The qualifying tenant joined the RTM Company days after the claim notice and supported the claim. Section 79(2) prescribes no express consequence of invalidity. The court should therefore identify the consequence Parliament intended by looking at the purpose of the rule and the facts, applying R v Soneji. Sections 78(7) and 81(1) show that Parliament provided expressly for invalidity where it intended it. Section 107 gives a discretionary enforcement remedy to any interested person. Treating the claim notice as void would produce uncertainty, and the statutory scheme is intended to keep opportunities for obstruction by landlords to a minimum. The statement in A1 Properties at para 69 was obiter, because that case concerned section 79(6) and the question was reserved. It should not be followed.
respondent_submissions: The Freeholder argues that section 78(1) requires a NIP to be given to every eligible qualifying tenant before a claim is made. Section 79(2) then states expressly what follows from non-compliance: the claim notice may not be given. A notice given in breach is therefore invalid or void, and no claim based on it can succeed. Because Parliament has stated the consequence expressly, there is no room for the more nuanced Soneji analysis. The language is mandatory. The Supreme Court said in A1 Properties at para 69 that section 79(2) imposes a clear consequence, namely that no valid claim notice can be given to anyone. It said much the same in Settlers Court at para 16. Those statements are part of the ratio or are at least highly persuasive, as the Court of Appeal held. The Freeholder further says that a qualifying tenant can easily be given a NIP by posting it to each flat. The scheme is designed to ensure that the right to manage is acquired only after all qualifying tenants have been invited to participate. If absolute invalidity is unworkable, the Freeholder submits in the alternative that the claim notice is valid for procedural purposes such as fixing the relevant date but invalid for the purpose of pursuing a successful claim.
legal_materials: Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Act 2002, Chapter 1 of Part 2. Section 78(1): before making a claim, an RTM company must give notice to each person who is a qualifying tenant of a flat in the premises and neither is nor has agreed to become a member of the company. Section 78(7): a NIP is not invalidated by inaccuracy in its particulars. Section 79(2): the claim notice may not be given unless each person required to be given a NIP has been given one at least 14 days before. Section 79(8): a copy of the claim notice must be given to every qualifying tenant. Section 81(1): a claim notice is not invalidated by inaccuracy in its particulars. Section 84(1) and (2): only the persons listed in section 79(6) may give a counter-notice, which must either admit that the RTM company was on the relevant date entitled to acquire the right to manage, or allege that by reason of a specified provision of the Chapter it was not so entitled. Section 107: discretionary power to order a person to make good a failure to comply with the Chapter. Authorities: R v Soneji [2005] UKHL 49; A1 Properties (Sunderland) Ltd v Tudor Studios RTM Co Ltd [2024] UKSC 27; Settlers Court RTM Co Ltd v FirstPort Property Services Ltd [2022] UKSC 1; Elim Court RTM Co Ltd v Avon Freeholds Ltd [2017] EWCA Civ 89.
actual_reasoning_summary: The Supreme Court held that breach of sections 78(1) and 79(2) does not invalidate the claim notice and cannot found a counter-notice objection to entitlement. Applying the Soneji principle, section 79(2) is a timing rule for claim notices and not an express sanction for breach of section 78(1). The scheme divides into substantive entitlement conditions, which alone can ground a dispute about entitlement under section 84, and a procedural code. The NIP rules are procedural and protect qualifying tenants, who have no right to object. The Freeholder was not protected by them and suffered no prejudice. The proper remedy is a discretionary order under section 107. The statement in A1 Properties at para 69 was not part of the ratio and should not be followed, so the Upper Tribunal's decision was restored.
outcome_evidence: Para 81: "For those reasons I would allow this appeal, and restore the decision of the Upper Tribunal." Para 65 states the conclusion: "the statutory scheme in the 2002 Act does not impose invalidity of the claim notice as the sanction for breach of either or both of sections 78(1) and 79(2)." Lord Briggs gave the judgment, with which Lord Reed, Lord Stephens, Lady Rose and Lord Snowden agreed.
